The flaw is that the capital's actual fall happens in two summary paragraphs [22]–[23] while the camera stays on oxen and records.
episodes.best: 'You honour me, Majesty. …Which seat?' / 'Ha! Listen to him. Which seat! Take your pick. I've got forty-one of them.' [45]–[46]
episodes.worst: [50]–[60]: seven quotes, then a detached 'Nobody counts them' with no antecedent, then a repeat of the Falling Flowers naming. The momentum dies right after the episode's best scene.
fixes: Open on Euija hearing about Gyebek. One short scene before the oxen pays off #4, #56 and #66, and it is the beat the whole thread has been building toward.
Cut [50]–[55] and the duplicate outburst [18]–[20]. Move [57]–[60] to follow [29] as the two maids' last beat.

Fire the #18 plant inside the Ye Sikjin scene: at [48], Euija understands, and the narrator (or Euija) says 'Nobody inspects the evidence for a thing they already want to believe.' Then expand the Chunchu–Euija feast [63]–[70] and give Gumil one face-to-face line.

episodes.title: Buyeo Euija†
episodes.verdict: The confession scene is the best Euija since #4, and his last lines are earned. Cut the duplicated curse, actually show the life that 'flashes before his eyes', and shrink the six-paragraph eulogy to the two paragraphs that bite.
episodes.best: 'Ten thousand? I'm sixty. Ambitious fellow, your clerk.' [5]; and 'Any last words?' … 'No.' [21]–[23]
episodes.worst: [28]–[41]: 'His life flashes before his eyes' with nothing shown, three summary lines that repeat the curse, then a six-paragraph eulogy.
fixes: Replace [28]–[31] with the flashback the narration promises: three or four lines from #4 (the hedge, the river, 'Nineteen', the name), ending on Gyebek.
Cut [1]–[2], [9]–[11] and the eulogy down to [39]–[40]. The episode should run confession, curse, messengers, Gyebek, end.

Keep #18's promise word for word at [20]: 'Gods are props. Spirits are lighting.' / 'Heh… so you guys are real after all…' Then give Kangrim his binary, e.g. 'Were you the Zengzi of the East, or the man who faked the dragon?', and let Euija's answer be his last joke.

episodes.title: Kim Chunchu†
episodes.verdict: A tender father–son deathbed that pays off the book's title. It's weakened by a doubled opening, duplicated lines, a cryptic Kangrim, and the same name-read-three-times-plus-italic-eulogy template #74 used one episode earlier.
episodes.romance: Munhee and Chunchu get one exchange, 'Have I… paid all of it?' / 'Not yet. I'll pay the rest.' [6]–[7], and it carries a whole marriage. One more beat between them before Bupmin enters would make it a goodbye rather than a handoff.
episodes.best: 'Munhee. Have I… paid all of it?' / 'Not yet. I'll pay the rest.' [6]–[7]
episodes.worst: [17]–[23]. Kangrim's scene is a string of riddles ('The West is already in the hall', 'the packing list is his', 'Walk, Spring-and-Autumn') with a duplicated sentence, and a first-time reader can't tell what was asked or answered.
fixes: Give Kangrim the binary the scene has already built: 'Was it for Gotaso, or for the king for all?' Let Chunchu answer 'Yes.' Cut the West and packing riddles [20]–[22].
Cut the double opening [0]–[2], the duplicate [19], and the widget tail [34]–[36].
Drop the italic eulogy, since #74 just used the form, or reduce it to [30] and [32] in plain narration.

episodes.title: Ungjin Commandery
episodes.verdict: A transitional collage with no protagonist and no Baekje point of view: three witty vignettes, then three widgets and an archival edict. It needs one through-line, ideally the first Baekje rebel, to start the restoration question its card promises.
episodes.best: 'Then sign as its clerk, Majesty. / And keep a copy.' [13]
episodes.worst: [24]–[29]: another invasion of Goguryeo announced in one line, then three widgets and an edict. Nobody on screen wants anything.
fixes: Add a Baekje point of view. One scene of Boksin's rebels, or Boksin tearing down a posted Tang calendar, gives the restoration its first face and sets up #77's 'He raised a dead country once'.
Cut [2]–[3] and [25]–[27], and paraphrase the edict [29] into two lines.
Link the vignettes through the calendar and taboo-name list Liu Rengui brings ([5], [7]–[9]). It is already the episode's best idea, and it echoes Euija's 'a country is a story'.

episodes.title: King Pungjang
episodes.verdict: The Asuka scene and the roll call are a delightful reset with a clear new question: the crown is Pung's, the army is Boksin's. Three flashbacks, four repeated lines, a spoiler and two archival speeches bury it, and Pung never mentions his father.
episodes.battle: No battle, but the roll call [9]–[41] does what a pre-battle muster should. Each captain gets a distinct body and one trait (Abe loud, Echi devoted, Dochim serene, Sangji a wall, Sangya the money, Boksin the board). It sets out a chain-of-command problem [41] and an enemy watching from the ridge [40], and it sets up #83 well. Its only flaw is that [0.7] has already told the reader how the war ends.

episodes.worst: [42]–[56]: an out-of-place 643 spy flashback, four blocks repeating one idea (one with a misattributed quote), and the Pisong move told before it is argued, in two archival walls.
fixes: Cut [0.1]–[0.2], [6.12]–[7], [42]–[46] and [53], and play Pisong [54]–[55] as a six-line argument between Pung and Echi. The episode becomes Asuka, the beach, the walls, and the first fight over the crown.
Connect Pung to Euija: one line calling back 'Until I need you' (#18 [74]), and Boksin naming the dying wish (#74 [17]). That gives the restoration its emotional reason.
Remove the spoilers: [0.7]'s 'forty-two thousand men to die in a river' and [43]'s 'They will do it to each other unassisted'.

episodes.title: Pyongyang I
episodes.verdict: A title that promises a siege delivers a chronicle; stage one real scene at the walls and cut the duplicate quotes.
episodes.battle: The frozen-river rout is the only fighting and it is reported, not shown: no POV inside it, no plan beyond 'it froze', cost given as a number [12]–[14]. The best beat is the aftermath, Yeon's "It freezes every year" [16], which is character, not battle.
episodes.best: "Don't tell me you didn't know it would freeze. It freezes every year." [16]
episodes.worst: [12]–[14]: one rout told three times with the same numbers.
fixes: Cut [8] and [14] (and trim [13]); those beats are already narrated or played.
Build the gate meeting [15]–[16] into a real exchange between Yeon and Namseng, so the episode titled Pyongyang has a scene at Pyongyang.

episodes.title: Snake River
episodes.verdict: The thirteen-sons count is a set piece readers will remember, but the episode braids four stories and rewinds mid-way; tighten the prose and put the reaper scene where it happened.
episodes.battle: The best-staged fight in the first half of the slice: one POV (Yeon), a clear device (the count), escalating obstacles (the archer, the bargainer, the flag-bearer), and a cost the enemy feels. Weak on stakes and geography: the White Tiger is a stranger, so his sons' deaths carry horror but not grief, and the ambush itself (the Tang host, the plan) is never shown [0]–[2].

episodes.worst: [34]–[39]: the Xue interlude plus the rewind, between the climax and the near-death that should precede it.

Plant the White Tiger and his sons in #78 so the count has a face.
Prune the count's aphorisms by a third and cut quote [31].

episodes.title: Tamla Surrenders
episodes.verdict: A 186-word stub that buries a beloved character's payoff inside a quote; merge it into #81 or dramatize Yuri Dora's choice.

episodes.verdict: A clean little court story with a real decision and a plant; cut the two-Jinjus lecture and it works.

Retitle the episode: there is no rebellion on the page ("Sick Leave" is already the scene title).

episodes.worst: [14]–[15]: the betrayal the episode is named for happens in one summary sentence.

episodes.title: White River
episodes.verdict: The best-built battle in the slice (plan, tide, reversal, cost, a brother on each side), held back by a numbers-heavy opening and a summarized aftermath.

POV: split between the Black Tortoise, the patient strategist we watch think [33]–[36], and Takutsu, whose death pays off #77. Plan and reversal are clear: hold, don't chase, wait for the tide, close the wings like a door with two leaves [45]. Cost: four hundred ships, Takutsu, Pung's sword. The brothers' sword beat [56]–[60] is the emotional payoff. Weaknesses: the turn is told, not played, and Silla is decoration (Munmu's charge [27]–[28] is fun but disconnected).
episodes.best: "He was always better at being sent away than I was." [60]
episodes.worst: [4]–[9]: a roll call of numbers before the first scene.

Play the tide's turn [43]–[45] from one deck instead of summarizing it.
Cut Yushin's caption line [30] and give the Sangji defection [66] one beat on the page.

episodes.title: Yeon Gesomun†

Give Yeon one last act of will before Yumla takes him (a callback to #29's vow), and put Gulgul silently in the room as a plant for #98.

Give the brothers one real face-to-face moment (at the gate or after the fall), using Namsan or cutting his card.
Fix [39], and put Gulgul in the burning palace snapping off the gold branch (one line) to plant #98.

episodes.title: Mount Gain

episodes.best: "I'm seventy, Majesty. I've buried three. Find me a war instead." [30]
episodes.worst: [24]: a wall of record between the oath and the ride home.

Cut the COVENANT block [24] and quote [11].
Pay off the temple copy [23] in #97 and give Yung one last appearance before the war ends.

[17]), and a cost and payoff (the stolen seal [27]–[29], marriage, Dangun). The explicit beats [23]–[25] are tender and brief. The best romance in the slice.

Trim the Joseon cast to two named people.
Give #87's ending a line that motivates the jump.

episodes.verdict: A record-heavy sketch whose protagonist has three contradictory identities; cut a quote and dramatize the quarrel.

episodes.worst: [2]–[4]: three versions of who Anseung is in three blocks.

Rewrite the card [15] (e.g. Munmu has had twenty years to draft the answer).

episodes.best: "Nowhere in it is the word 'sorry.'" / "Nowhere in it is the word 'rice.'" [24]–[25]
episodes.worst: [14]–[17]: two record blocks sit inside the speech and blunt its rhythm.

Pay off "Tell him I said his name" [21]: Inmun should appear before the war ends.
Make Daeto's arrest a scene rather than a funeral aside in #93.

episodes.worst: [3]–[7]: a battle that is only a map, two quotes and a formation card.
fixes: Dramatize the chase into Seokmun from Wonsul's POV, including Danneung holding his bridle (now a quote in #92 [1]).
Cut quote [6] and the commander names in [5].
Add one narrator line before the flashback so the reader suspects the apology is a move.

episodes.title: Wonsul
episodes.verdict: Strong lines for Yushin, but the reader meets Wonsul only after his shame, and the key moment lives in a quote.

episodes.worst: [0]–[1]: the whole arc summarized, then quoted.
fixes: Move Danneung and the bridle into #91 as a scene; cut [1].
Have Munmu answer [8] with his own boyhood "Retreat" (#10 [28]).
Trim [0] to its first two sentences.

episodes.title: Kim Yushin†
episodes.verdict: The death mostly lands (Kangrim, the 108 draws, "I wanted in", Munhee's question), but an obituary says it all a third time and the book's opening promises are too quiet.

episodes.worst: [25]–[32]: the burial, a stray traitor, and a five-paragraph essay between Munhee's question and Lady Jiso.

Make #1's promises audible: one clause at [14]–[15] that nobody has said his bare name in forty-one years, and the east star from #1 [47] over the house that night.

episodes.verdict: The oracle and Dangun are the right beats, but the episode replays #42's meet-cute as if it never happened, swings into explicit comedy right after a funeral, and tells the war's ending in advance.

Rewrite [0] so it doesn't repeat the #93 card.

episodes.title: Maeso
episodes.verdict: The best war-craft in the Silla–Tang arc (two real plans and a great punchline), but the traitor-pilot who opens it never appears, and Wonsul's redemption is summarized and then quoted.

Reversal and cost are clear ("For a farmer, losing horses… is like losing the field" [28]). Missing: a POV inside either fight that the reader cares about; Wonsul's horse-cut is narrated after the fact [24].

Cut [36]–[37], or turn [37] into a one-line wink.

Bookend the 660 landing (#72) in one line at [3].
Cut [11] and [16].

episodes.worst: [13]–[16]: the king for all dies in a sentence and a quote.

Close the race from #29 in a few lines (Euija's "a king, or a slave", Yeon's vow, the eastern star), and make [22] name the story the Tang court remembers.

episodes.title: Balhae
episodes.verdict: A moving father-son scene that pays off a plant from #7; the last page deflates it with a flash-forward, two quotes and a textbook era label.
episodes.best: "I took it. Nobody else was going to." [15]
episodes.worst: [33]–[38]: the book's last page is a quote and an era label.
fixes: End on [31], or on a short narrator coda that ties Balhae to the title (two kingdoms under one sky, each claiming it); cut [35]–[37].
Compress the replayed flashback [22.0]–[22.4].
Plant Gulgul in the endgame (Yeon's deathbed in #84 or the burning palace in #86).

arcs.throughline: On paper the arc has a smart skeleton. There are three pilots, one per kingdom (Silla #1–2, Baekje #4–5, Goguryeo #7–8), each satirising that kingdom's system: birth rank and a council that must agree; eight clans and an assembly for sale; five generals counting grain. Each is followed by a flashback to its greatest king whose glory becomes the next kingdom's grudge (Jinheung → Baekje, Geunchogo → Goguryeo, Gwanggaeto → Silla). By #8 a reader can tell the three kingdoms apart by texture, which is a real achievement. The title vow recurs in all three: Chunchu's 'one king for all' (#1 [47.5]), Euija's cut-off 'A king should be for the country—' (#4 [34]), King Youngryu's 'I will be the King for All' (#8 [9]). But a reader can't see the skeleton. The grudges live only in next-episode cards; no present-day character feels another kingdom; the narrator never points at the shared vow; and the shared threat is split between an uncarded 'Second Emperor' (#1) and 'the Tang' (#7), never linked. There is also no one to follow for long: Sunduk next speaks at #13, Euija and Gyebek at #18, Yeon at #15. Time runs backwards for the first three episodes (the coronation, the night before, decades before, with 612 flashbacks inside #1 and #2), and the year changes at six of the nine seams. A reader who gets through #1 will love #4 and enjoy #7; #5, #6 and the flashback stubs are where they drift. Plants that do work: Samsin's joke (#4 [3]) becomes a goddess at #8 [39]; Bupmin's 'I'm following' (#1 [20]) pays off at #10 [28]; Gusesa's 'Nephew. Sit down.' (#8 [26]) pays off at #24.

handoffs.why: The prologue blurb promises satire of 'the social systems of each of the Three Kingdoms', which #1–#8 deliver, and the Part title and #1's map frame three kingdoms. But nothing tells the reader whom to follow, and #1 spends its first narration on Munhee's hair [4] and its first twenty blocks on Chunchu's children before the queen appears.
handoffs.fix: Make #1's first scene Sunduk's, and let the map caption [1] or the narrator name the three kingdoms and the vow in one breath.

handoffs.why: The card's 'How? Go back one night, to a brazier' raises exactly the question #2 answers, at the place #1 [31] planted ('six men and a brazier').

One structural move used four times: a government lecture plus quote, term card and diagram or table before the scene starts (#1 [23]–[28], #5 [2]–[11] and [28]–[38], #8 [3]–[7]). And #3, #6 and #9 share one template: a great king, a stele or annal quote, a herald's aside, and a closing line that some kingdom does not forget.
top_problems: #1 is the weakest possible front door. About twenty named people and a dozen new places and terms in one episode. The title character speaks first at [29] with no introduction and is then called 'Dukman' without being told that's her. Three domestic scenes come before any conflict. The hook 'A Queen? Ridiculous.' is never dramatized, and the coronation happens in one line [35], sandwiched between a bone-rank lecture and an office table.

Three unrelated pilots. The connections exist only in next-episode cards (the grudge triangle) and in a vow nobody points at ('a king for all' in #1, #4 and #8). No present-day character feels another kingdom: #4 never mentions Silla, and #7–#8 touch it only through 'Yushin's banners'. The shared antagonist is split between an uncarded 'Second Emperor' in #1 and 'the Tang' in #7, never linked.

Explainer piles stall every 'system' episode: #5 opens with a quote and nine term cards, and the same pattern runs through #8 [3]–[7], #1 [23]–[28] and [37]–[38], #2 [1]–[11] (one rule told six times) and #7 [8]–[10] (one fact told three times). Records are 20–32% of #1, #2, #5, #7 and #8, and 25–57% of the three flashbacks.

The payoffs that matter happen off-page or in summary: Gyebek beating the Jinmo boy (#5 [24], four sentences), the 'no' votes flipping (#2 [22]→[27]), the crowning (#1 [35]), a king dying on his own wall (#6, two duplicate annal quotes).

Momentum drains after #4. Its heroes vanish (Euija has no lines in #5 and doesn't speak again until #18), and three flashback stubs with no scene and no character (#3, #6, #9; 276–602 words) sit between the pilots while the year changes at six of nine seams. Fold the stubs into their neighbours, or give each one a scene.

arcs.throughline: There is a spine, but it’s buried. The spine is Daeya: Silla marries its princess into a border fort (#12–13), and Baekje’s new king picks that same fort to make his name (#18–20). The convergence is strong and pays off hard in #23 (“We will be happy forever.” / “I am the one who made him swear it.”), but the slice never says it out loud. Five episodes separate Gotaso’s cart (#13 [23]) from Euija’s “Daeya… how about it?” (#19 [37]). Three of them are a Goguryeo side-arc (#15–17) that feeds Yeon’s coup in #24 rather than Daeya, and no narrator line joins the two threads. The arc’s title promise, the Five Principles, drives #10–11 and is then dropped. In practice this is three households (Chunchu’s, Yeon’s and Euija’s), with Chunchu’s family closest to the reader’s heart. A first-time reader keeps going on #11, the empty hall in #13, #17, and Euija’s voice in #18–19. The places they might stop are #10’s explainer opening, #14’s long bedroom passage and #16. Against the author’s suspicion, #11 Sadaham reads at nearly Prince Euija level, and #17 and #18 are strong.

Gotaso and Pumsuk move to Daeya (#13 [23]–[24]); Euija picks Daeya five episodes later (#19 [37], [45]) with no wink to the reader; and #21 makes the reader wade through about 4,300 words of goddess cavern before the march arrives. Records and explainer widgets stall openings and turns, often in duplicate: #10 [17]–[24], #16 [6]–[8], #17 [11]–[12], #18 [1]–[2], #19 [18]–[20], #20 [1]–[8], #11 [15]–[16]. A first-time reader meets the same fact twice in a row in five of these eleven episodes.

Both romances skip the scenes that would make us root for the couple. The father-asks-the-boy vow is summarized (#13 [1]–[7]). Pumsuk has no voice or flaw on the page (#12 [39]–[57]), though #21 depends on one. #14’s pyre has no Munhee in it and a doubled confession ([38], [47]), and ‘The Closed Months’ (#14 [50]–[67]) repeats one beat for eighteen blocks. The best-played love stories here are the side ones: Sadaham and Mugwan, and Sunduk and Yushin.

Timeline slips a careful reader trips on. Gotaso is 16 two springs apart (#12 [3], [27]). #13 hops forward to Daeya and back, then to ‘Earlier that evening’. #14’s ‘Years later’ birth blurs which child the pregnancy was, and ‘stopped going to the hill’ contradicts #1 [10]. #13 [64] has taverns arguing about Hundred-Victories while #18 [64] says nobody calls him that yet. #17’s ‘late in the year’ is followed by #18 in March.

arcs.throughline: There is a spine, and it’s Chunchu’s. Daeya takes his daughter (#23), he walks into Yeon’s hall and spends his own hand (#25–#26), and he comes home wanting the crown (#29). Yeon’s rise (#24, #27) runs beside it. The spine’s best scenes are some of the best in the book: the go-stone line (#23 [59]), the bloody hand, the planet callback. #27 Nangbi and much of #24–#25 come close to Prince Euija’s standard. But the arc opens with about 7,000 words (#21’s cavern and all of #22) of erotica that never touches the war, after making the reader wait 93 blocks for the Gumil the previous card promised. The war year’s one siege happens offstage, and Chunchu’s grief, the real engine, gets about 430 words. A reader who survives #21–#22 is rewarded by #24–#27; many won’t survive them.

top_problems: Sex and cavern scenes take roughly 8,300 of the slice’s ~18,600 words (#21 [0]–[92] ≈4,000; #22 ≈3,200; #23 [5]–[10] and [67]–[84] ≈730; #28 [14]–[25]; #26 [53]–[62]). They don’t move the war, they repeat the same beats in porn-parody register, and they break the arc’s K-drama-tragedy tone. #21 makes the reader wait 93 blocks for the Gumil that #20’s card promised. This, not the history, is why #21 and #22 are long, and their length isn’t earned.

The war year’s battles are summarized. Daeya falls in about 130 words (#23 [18]–[25]) with no geography, POV, plan or staged reversal; Jukjuk’s stand is only quoted; Gotaso’s death, Pumsuk’s surrender and the news arrive in a scrambled order (#23 [27]–[47]). #28’s forty fortresses are one sentence.

Gumil, the traitor whose choice drives the arc, is a cipher: three lines of grievance (#21 [98]–[100]), two of banter, then humiliation comedy (#23 [5]–[10]). The marriage-and-rank tragedy (#21 [104]–[108], [125]–[126]; #23 [11]–[17]) gets a few hundred words against about 7,000 for the cavern and Pumsuk’s night. Maehwa vanishes after #23 [17].

Continuity and chronology in the back half: #25’s release is told out of order and the rabbit letter never fires; #26 opens with a copy of #25 [2]; #28 contradicts #26 [39] and #31 [43] on who is taking forty fortresses, jumps to 645, then #29 returns to 642; #30 is a stub that #31 replays.

Record and explainer pile-ups right after the best scenes: #24 [36]–[61] (five records, three cards, a diagram), #23 [50]–[54] (two records and a map inside Chunchu’s grief), #26 [38]–[39], #28 [6] and [13], and #30 [2]–[4] (72% records).

arcs.throughline: The Seventh Invasion has a spine on paper (the greatest emperor alive rolls over Goguryeo's forts and is stopped by one small wall and a man nobody wrote down) and a superb motif that ties it to the Jumong arc: names. The emperor whose name may not be said (#31 [3]–[8]), the Guardian nobody recorded (#32 [17]–[18], #36 [2], [35]), Yuhwa trading her name for a god's descent (#37 [23]–[24], [49]), Habek's 'Say a name' (#37 [55]), Sosuno giving hers at the well (#39 [131]). But nobody carries the invasion. The emperor is a voice between quotes; the Guardian has about a dozen lines across two episodes; Yeon Gesomun, whose regicide is the excuse and who closed Part I vowing to forge a country 'with my own hands' (#29 [21]), gets one unlocated line after the war is over (#36 [34]); and the battles are filed as summaries and duplicate records. (a) Battles: Yodong, the rest of the line and Stallion Mountain are summaries told from the invader's side; only Ansi's earthen mountain is dramatized, with geography, a plan and a reversal, and its climax then dissolves into weather. (b) Flashbacks: #33 and #35 are record dumps (47% and 76% records) that interrupt the invasion at its two turning points without changing anything in 645. The Jumong detour is set up (the Yodong shrine bride, 'Holy King, look down', Gesomun's cave in #29) and doesn't strand the siege's suspense, because Ansi already ended in #36. But that suspense was spent early by the Tang clerks (#36 [4]–[5]) and resolved by the cold, and Ansi gets about 900 words while Jolbon's courtship alone runs about 2,700. After 9,250 words of myth the story never returns to Goguryeo; #40 opens in Silla, so the invasion arc has no closing beat. (c) The Jumong arc is the most alive writing in the slice: a real seduction game, a chase with jokes, a tsundere romance with an earned confession, and long-range plants that pay (the turtle joke, the three-legged crow, Yeon Tabal). It isn't yet the equal of Prince Euija. #37 skips Haemosu's side of the cost, #38 smothers its climax in three quotes, and #39 is a 3,000-word story in 5,200 words with five codas. Cut #39 by 40% and the author's claim holds. A first-time reader stays for the human inserts in #31–#36 (the shrine bride, Sul Gedu, the Yeon boys, the earthen mountain), skims the records, and is pulled hard through #37–#38 until #39's middle.

Who was he?') is planted by the Yodong shrine bride (#32 [9]–[12]), 'Holy King, look down' (#34 [35]) and Gesomun's cave (#29 [18]–[21]). top_problems: The invasion is filed, not dramatized. Its battles are one-paragraph roll-ups plus duplicate records (Yodong #32 [14]; the rest of the line #32 [23]–[25]; Stallion Mountain #34 [12]–[16]). The POV belongs to the invader (the emperor, Xue Rengui, Sul Gedu), Goguryeo's defenders are faceless apart from the Guardian's dozen lines, and Yeon Gesomun, the war's cause, gets one unlocated line after it's over (#36 [34]).

Ansi's climax deflates. The outcome is spoiled by the clerks at #36 [4]–[5]; the emperor's wounding is an image-prompt fragment ([26] 'Sweat. Yellow camp light.'); the retreat is weather told in one line ([28]–[29]); and the arc's best plants pay off as a quote or not at all: the dead minister's 'no' (#31 [12] → #36 [31]), the torn-up road (#32 [5]), and the two nameless men who never confront each other over names.

#39 Jolbon is a 3,000-word story in 5,200 words: the tsundere loop [57]–[82], four bedroom sequences repeating the 'Little Sosuno' joke, a summarized founding [205]–[214], the Pine Kingdom errand [228]–[238], and five codas [240]–[257] that spoil #67 (Sosuno's 'second country', 'the year Yuri comes south'). #31 overloads a first-time reader and has no protagonist: eight vignettes and about twenty named people (one minister with two titles, a herald who answers himself, four generals in a Korean-only table, the 'Prince of Qin', Xue Rengui suddenly called 'Xue Li'), the army mustering before anyone is called up, and a Longmen scene buried under an edict, three quotes and two asides.

arcs.throughline: Yes, and it's the best spine in this slice; the author's hunch holds. Bidam's rebellion plays as a four-act thriller. Want (#40): stop a soft successor and Chunchu's 'Tang envelope'. Escalation on a clock (#42): ten days of palace grain and five nights of tea that curdle from courtesy to 'you were never even of Silla'. Reversal (#44): heaven's omen turned with a burning kite and paid for with Hangyul. Cost (#46): the 109th bout, Bidam's house erased in his own words, the queen dead the same night. It starts as Bidam's story and ends as Yushin's, and that handoff works because Yushin ends it with Bidam's line. Its best beats (the veto, the rant, Hangyul, 'One hundred and nine. Finally.', 'Dukman') are as good as anything in Prince Euija. Three things hold every episode at 3–4. (1) The interleaved flashbacks: #43 earns its slot (short, it answers the taunt, its card returns to the siege); #41 and #45 don't, and between them they take 5,900 of the arc's 15,900 words at its two tensest moments. (2) The fighting is summarised: the siege gets one sentence of combat, the duel two. (3) The setup is thin: before #40 the friendship is one short exchange and the 108 score in #2, Seungman is one sentence in #1, and Bidam and Sunduk never share a scene, so the queen 'between them' is only Yushin's. Romance is the arc's quiet strength (Seohyun and Manmyung; the deathbed); battle is its weakness. A reader keeps going through #40, #42, #44 and #46, and skims #41 and the back half of #45. The titles Gi/Seung/Jeon/Gyeol don't tell a first-time reader these four are one story: add 'Bidam's Rebellion' to them.

top_problems: The flashbacks break the thriller at its two tensest points. #41 Suro (1,800 words of myth and sex, no conflict) comes one block after Bidam decides to rebel; #45 Seohyun (4,100 words, the slice's longest) sits between Day 9 and Day 10, after Seohyun's ghost has already spoken in #44, and a quarter of it replays #21. Take #41 out of the arc, and run a trimmed #45 after #43.

The climax is summarised and scrambled. Ten days of siege get one sentence of combat (#44 [80]); the duel is two sentences (#46 [8]–[9]); Bidam dies at [14], speaks at [28] and falls again at [29]; and a record [25] says he fled and was beheaded.

The rivalry and the triangle are back-filled inside the arc. Before #40, Bidam and Yushin share one short exchange (#2 [31]–[33], 38 episodes earlier), Seungman gets one sentence (#1 [30]), and Bidam and Sunduk never share a scene. Five short flashbacks in #40–#46 have to build the friendship while the plot breaks it, and the queen in the middle is only Yushin's.

Bidam's want shifts and his endgame is never stated: merit (#40 [38]), anti-Tang (#40 [40]), 'A woman cannot rule well' (#42 [17]), blood (#42 [29]), soil (#44 [87]). The radicalisation is deliberate, but nobody says what winning looks like, and the misogynist banner raised by the man who crowned a woman is never owned on the page.

Muddled plants and contradictions undercut the payoffs: the headband (kept, given, refused), Seungman as sister and cousin, Yushin as 'elder brother', 'the opposite kite', a 'twist' labelled 'the first day of the rebellion', and Muryuk's name already on screen as a speaker label in #20.

arcs.throughline: Yes for #48–#51: this is Chunchu’s rise. He goes west for an army, falls for the emperor’s one-brush machine, builds his own, loses the emperor and his promise, and takes the chair he has avoided since #2, with Li Zhi and Wu as a Tang subplot that keeps paying (gyuku and the gate in #48, the deathbed and the nunnery in #50, the letter in #51). A first-time reader keeps going through #51 on the Second Emperor, Chunchu’s wit and the Saluzi and name mysteries, although the biggest moments are told rather than played. The spine breaks after #51. The war question the coronation raises (a ‘private grudge’ against Baekje) is shelved for four backward episodes: #52 in 644, then three founding myths, about 2,900 words. #56 then resumes with Baekje leads last on stage at #29, and seven more myth episodes (#57–#63) follow it, so from #52 to #63 only #56 is set in the present (about 11,000 words). The out-of-order years don’t lose a reader about when, because every card signposts its jump; they cost cause and effect (#49 before #50) and momentum (#52–#55).

top_problems: Huangdi (#48) is 7,900 words with its central question spent early: a quote at [36] says Tang ‘promised to send an army’, and the next 230 blocks ride on two excellent mystery boxes (Saluzi, the emperor’s name) through about 2,000 words of detour. That detour is the First Emperor flashback [82], the Gija & Wiman flashback [210]–[211], the History Office and Academy tails, a duplicate Wu scene [195]–[204], two extra horses and 12 explainer widgets. Cut about 1,500 words and hold the emperor’s yes until the Six Steeds, or split at [177].

The slice tells its biggest moments instead of playing them. The emperor’s dying is a stage direction (#48 [167]) and his death happens between episodes (#50 [1]). Chunchu’s coronation, the end of a thread running since #2, is a summary sentence, an unattributed quote and emoji speakers (#51 [10]–[15]). On Gunhae dies in four blocks with no reaction (#48 [262]–[264]), and Tang’s threat to Baekje is a 300-word edict nobody receives (#49 [52]).

The chronology costs cause and effect, not orientation; every card signposts its jump. But #49 (651) shows the new emperor’s calendar and edict before #50 (649) shows the old one die and Chunchu decide ‘Then it is mine’, so swap them. After #51 raises the Baekje war, four backward episodes (#52 in 644, then three myths, about 2,900 words) stall the present, with seven Tamla myth episodes (#57–#63) right behind #56: from #52 to #63 only #56 is set in the present.

Records restate scenes. About 20 of the slice’s 26 quote blocks repeat the paragraph or dialogue right before them, and #49 is 42% records, ending on a 300-word edict. The myths suffer most: #54 has five quotes in a comedy, #55 three in twelve blocks.

The myth triad doesn’t make its point or lead anywhere. Hyukgose, Talhae and Alji are Silla’s three royal houses (Park, Seok, Kim), told right after the first True Bone Kim takes the throne, but Park is never named, Chunchu is never linked to Alji, #53 opens on a garbled sentence about an unexplained ‘Old Joseon’, and nothing in them sets up Gyebek’s exile in #56. Frame them with Chunchu (a new king at the founder’s tombs), compress #53 and #55, or merge all three into one episode of about 1,800 words.

arcs.throughline: Two spines: Euija’s fall (the king who wanted to own Baekje’s story loses it to a better storyteller) and Gyebek’s exile and return (a literal man living on one promise). They are built to run in parallel but play in sequence with long detours, and the two men never share a scene in the slice (their last talk is #29). (a) Euija’s theme pays off brilliantly in #66: Muyeol forges the omens, Euija can’t expose them without exposing his own paper dragon, and says ‘Well made’; the river jump calls back #4. The personal arc does not pay off: his #56 motive vanishes in #64, the decline is a shot list instead of a choice, and ‘Summon Gyebek…!’ leads to no reunion. Gyebek’s character builds well (counting, literalness, ‘I trusted one man’), and the island tales plant what fires at #72 (Kangrim’s origin, choosing the ground, ten units of five hundred). But his two defining acts are not built: the family is never shown, and the vow #72 calls back is never spoken. (b) The jump into myth is motivated (Yuri Dora’s fire) and every tale keeps a Gyebek reaction. #57 and #62 connect strongly; #58–#61 connect only by theme and mostly in summary; #63 doesn’t connect at all. Seven in a row, right after three Silla myths (#53–#55), means 10 of the 11 episodes from #53 to #63 are myth, and Euija is offstage from #56 [80] to #64 (and had little page time since #29). Readers come back at #64 for the satire, not for Euija. (c) The suspense machinery toward the last stand is good (Seongchung’s two doors, Heungsu’s map, Ye Sikjin’s drawer, Muyeol’s rumour, ‘Mine is fixed’), but #67 and #71 cut away at the two peak moments, and the timeline of Gyebek’s return is knotted. A reader would keep going, mostly for #57, #64, #66, #69 and #70; the quitting risk is #58–#63 and #65.

top_problems: Structure: 9 of the 16 episodes are flashback or myth. #57–#63 run seven in a row right after three Silla myths (#53–#55), and #67 and #71 cut away at the two peak moments (right after ‘Summon Gyebek…!’, and between the march and the battle). Interleave the island evenings with the Sabi episodes, merge #63 into #59 and #68 into #69, and move #67 and #71.

The Euija–Gyebek bond, the heart of #4, has no scene: the two never meet on page from #56 to #72 (their last talk is #29). Euija’s #56 motive evaporates in #64, his decline is never a choice, and ‘Summon Gyebek…!’ (#66) leads to no reunion. Add a recall he writes and doesn’t send (#64), and a meeting, letter or token before the march (#70).

#65 [14]–[26]: thirteen paragraphs of image-prompt shot lists in the narration (‘They hike the silk. One knee up. A twist.’), the house rule’s own banned example. It is the most quit-worthy stretch in the slice and buries Euija’s decline. Cut to one paragraph.

Gyebek’s family killing (#70 [16]–[17]), the act #72’s Kangrim question hinges on, is one line and a record about a wife and children never mentioned in 70 episodes. Plant them in #56 and on the island.

Chronology and naming knots: #56 tells the exile three times out of order; #64 is dated 655 inside a three-year mourning that began in 655; #69’s ‘655 berth’ flashback has Gyebek marching to Yellow Mountain; #68 debates sending Gyebek while he is still on Tamla; and names double up (Tanhyeon/Chimhyeon, Rock of Politics/Deer Rock, Seongchung/Sungchung, Daebyeol/Big Star, five handles for three Sateks).

arcs.throughline: #72–#75 close Part II's three great lives (Gyebek, Euija, Chunchu) in four episodes; #76–#77 open the occupation and the restoration. The first half has a spine, the fall of Euija's Baekje, but its emotional centre is hollow. Euija is absent from Gyebek's last stand. The two never meet after #29, despite 'Summon Gyebek…!' in #66, and Euija never reacts to Gyebek's death. A reader keeps going for Yellow Mountain and the confession. After #75 the pull drops sharply until the roll call, because #76 has no protagonist and #77 never ties the restoration to the king who begged for it. The restoration does raise a question worth following in #77 (the crown is Pung's, the army is Boksin's), but it arrives late and is parked for Goguryeo at once.

top_problems: The Euija–Gyebek payoff happens off-page. There is no reunion after 'Summon Gyebek…!' (#66 [41]); Euija is absent from Yellow Mountain except for a flashback to a vow #4 never contained (#72 [120]); and #73 opens without any reaction to the death. The book's best relationship ends on one oblique '…A friend.' (#74 [26]).

Climaxes are cluttered and pre-spent. #72's outcome is announced by a widget [33], the duel is pre-spent in prompt fragments [26] and then summarized [61], the sons' deaths are foretold [88], and quotes retell what the scene just showed ([64]–[65], [107]). #73 stops for seven quotes [50]–[56]. #77 spends the White River [0.7], the restoration's self-destruction [43] and Pisong [53].

The deaths explain themselves. #74 and #75 run the same template and end in italic essays ([36]–[41], [28]–[32]). #74 announces 'His life flashes before his eyes' and shows nothing. Kangrim's question ritual is skipped for both kings.

The restoration starts without a heart. #76 has no point of view and no Baekje character. #77's lovely roll call sits between a textbook 371 flashback, an out-of-place 643 spy flashback, four repeated lines and two archival speeches, and Pung never mentions the father whose dying wish he is fulfilling.

Draft residue and continuity slips that a careful reader will trip on: a '?' speaker (#72 [91]); the Tang emperor's stray '?' (#72 [128]); Gyebek asking and answering himself (#72 [34]–[36]); Kangrim as 'heaven's messenger' against #62 [1]; the blood-ties line misattributed to Chunchu (#77 [44] against #64 [44]); Munhee's 'sister who was a queen' (#75 [5]); untranslated verse (#77 [0.2]); a hangul table (#76 [27]); 'Goryeo' (#76 [29]); 'Revival Society' (#77 [46]).

arcs.throughline: Three spines run in sequence: Goguryeo's fall (Yeon's last river, his death, his sons' war, #78–#86), Baekje's last stand (#80–#83), and Munmu's war against his Tang ally (#87–#97), with Balhae as the coda. Munmu is the nominal hero, but the vivid POVs are Yeon, Yushin and Xue; Munmu mostly receives letters and messengers. A reader keeps going through #79–#87 for the deaths, the bell and the horse, loses momentum in the record-heavy run #89–#91, and reaches a quiet, unclimactic finish (#96–#97) rescued by #98's cave. Overall the ending reads more like a summary than a climax: the deaths land (Yeon's wryly, Yushin's mostly), but the war the title depends on is won offstage, and the title episode never shows the king for all being one.

top_problems: The climaxes are told, not shown. Stone Gate (#91), the fall of Pyongyang (#86 [26]–[27]), Wonsul's redemption (#95 [24]–[25]) and Final Ford (#96 [10]–[16]) arrive as summaries, quotes, formation cards and messengers, and the war ends on "Have we… won…?" with its antagonist offstage. Record pile-ups (#80 75%, #91 47%, #89 43%, #78 42%) and narrated-played-quoted triple tellings stall the endgame.

#97 doesn't pay off the title. It skips the coronation, never shows the king for all acting on the six-year-old's sentence (#1 [12], #52 [15]), forgets the three-way race (#29), and gives Munmu a two-line death without Kangrim.
Planted threads vanish at the finish: Punghun (a name only), Xue (no exit, ancestors unburied), Inmun, Yung and the temple covenant, Yuri Dora, Pung, and Gulgul until the last episode.

Chronology and continuity breaks: the unmarked rewind from #86 (668) to #87 (665); #94 treating the goddesses as strangers despite #42; #86 [39] crediting Yushin with opening a city Shinsung opened; #79's reaper scene told out of order; #82's flashback running past #81.

Tone and spoilers: #94's explicit comedy right after Yushin's funeral; obituaries that decode the scene and spoil the next episode (#84 [28], #94 [27]); and a last page that ends on a textbook era label after the real ending ("Cut to black", #98 [31]).
